content: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is a zoonotic disease, with Leishmania infantum identified as the primary causative species. However, much of the available data on treatment and prevention comes from open-label, uncontrolled studies. Various treatment regimens have been employed, including pentavalent antimonials (20 mg/kg per day for 3–4 weeks), amphotericin B (liposomal or lipid complex formulations at 3–5 mg/kg per day for 3–4 weeks), and pentamidine (4 mg/kg per day, or 300 mg for adults, administered every 3–4 weeks). The effectiveness of secondary prophylaxis using amphotericin B lipid complex (3 mg/kg every 21 days) was evaluated in a single prospective randomized study, which compared it to no prophylaxis. The drug was well-tolerated, and after 12 months of follow-up, 22% of patients receiving prophylaxis experienced relapse, compared to 50% in the group without prophylaxis. A meta-analysis of available studies demonstrated a significant benefit of secondary prophylaxis in reducing VL relapse rates. The average relapse rate was 67% in patients without prophylaxis, compared to 31% in those receiving it. Most of the data came from regions endemic to L. infantum, where VL transmission is zoonotic. European studies suggest that a CD4 cell count greater than 100 cells/mm³ at the time of VL diagnosis reduces the likelihood of relapse. Consequently, for Spanish patients, a CD4 count threshold of 200–350 cells/mm³ has been proposed as a safe point for discontinuing secondary prophylaxis. In the Americas, liposomal amphotericin B is recommended for secondary prophylaxis in VL-HIV co-infected patients after the first VL episode, particularly in those with CD4 counts below 350 cells/mm³. This recommendation is based on strong consensus but very low-certainty evidence. In areas with anthroponotic transmission of Leishmania donovani, such as East Africa and Southeast Asia, the parasite appears to be more virulent. For example, in an Ethiopian study, 11 of 39 patients with relapse had CD4 counts above 200 cells/mm³ before relapse, whereas relapse was rare in European patients with CD4 counts above 100 cells/mm³. This difference may be attributed to the parasite's virulence, host immune responses, nutritional status, and co-existing infections or comorbidities. Despite greater clinical experience in managing VL-HIV co-infection in East Africa, evidence on secondary prophylaxis remains limited, and further studies are needed. Medical care for VL in HIV co-infected patients is severely constrained in both East Africa and Southeast Asia, with only a few tertiary centers managing these cases. Health systems in these regions often lack adequate surveillance, drug toxicity monitoring, and follow-up services. Additionally, the risk of drug resistance must be considered, as HIV co-infected patients may serve as reservoirs for drug-resistant L. donovani. To mitigate this risk, it is generally recommended to use a different drug for secondary prophylaxis than the one used for primary VL treatment. In East Africa, pentamidine has been used as secondary prophylaxis in HIV-positive VL patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/mm³ or in those with a history of relapse. Monthly infusions of 4 mg/kg pentamidine were administered for 12 months, starting one month after completing VL treatment and achieving parasitological cure. In one study, the probability of relapse-free survival was 79% at 6 months, 71% at 1 year, and 53% at 24–36 months. Serious adverse events were reported in 23% of patients, with renal failure being a potential side effect in two cases. Another study in Ethiopia reported a relapse-free survival rate of 46% at 12 months, with serious adverse events in 28% of patients. In Southeast Asia, limited data are available on secondary prophylaxis. A retrospective cohort study in India (2005–2015) compared patients receiving monthly amphotericin B (liposomal or deoxycholate formulations) to those without prophylaxis. At 1 year, none of the patients receiving prophylaxis relapsed, compared to 75% of controls. However, the evidence was considered very uncertain due to the study's limitations. The World Health Organization (WHO) conditionally recommends secondary prophylaxis after the first VL episode in HIV co-infected patients in East Africa. Pentamidine is the primary drug used in this region, offering additional benefits such as preventing Pneumocystis jirovecii infections. However, its cost and lack of a donation program for VL must be considered. In Southeast Asia, secondary prophylaxis is also recommended, but the evidence is insufficient to endorse a specific drug. Treatment outcomes for VL are assessed through clinical improvement and parasitological confirmation of cure. HIV co-infected patients should undergo parasitological testing at the end of treatment to confirm cure, as they are at higher risk of relapse. Follow-up is critical, with assessments at 6-month intervals to detect late relapses. Relapse in VL is defined as the recurrence of symptoms with parasitological confirmation after initial cure. Risk factors for relapse include low CD4 counts (<200 cells/mm³), failure to achieve parasitological cure, and lack of antiretroviral therapy (ART) or secondary prophylaxis. Treatment for relapse often involves repeating the same regimen or switching to alternative drugs, depending on the patient's clinical condition and drug availability. In cases of multiple relapses or non-responsiveness, compassionate treatment options may be considered, but clinicians must be cautious about the risk of drug resistance. Special considerations are required for pregnant women, children, and the elderly. Liposomal amphotericin B is the preferred treatment for VL in pregnant women, as other drugs, such as miltefosine, are contraindicated due to teratogenicity. For children, liposomal amphotericin B is also the safest option, although its use in combination therapy remains uncertain. In summary, secondary prophylaxis is a critical component of managing VL-HIV co-infection, particularly in high-burden regions. However, more research is needed to establish optimal treatment regimens, criteria for initiating and discontinuing prophylaxis, and strategies to address drug resistance and improve patient outcomes.
